title: Susceptibility Testing: Big Zone, Small MIC — and Mind the D
summary: Read an MIC and MBC, connect zone size to MIC, interpret results with organism-specific breakpoints that change every year, and catch inducible clindamycin resistance with the D-test.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 58 Hit 1 (MIC/MBC), Hit 3 (zone inversely related to MIC; species-specific breakpoints), Hit 4 (use current CLSI M100), Hit 7 (D-test), Trap 2 and the Figure 58 anchor. Checked against Hulankova 2024, Saar 2025, Yu 2026, Shoman & Radwan 2026, Addis 2025 and Rossi 2026. Pending: CLSI wording “report clindamycin resistant” for a positive D-test; broth microdilution conditions (Hit 2).

objectives: Define MIC and MBC and read them from a dilution series.
Explain the inverse relationship between zone diameter and MIC and the role of organism-specific breakpoints.
Perform and interpret the D-test for inducible clindamycin resistance.

scenes.title: “Clindamycin susceptible” — and the infection got worse
scenes.altText: A Staphylococcus aureus skin abscess isolate: erythromycin resistant, clindamycin susceptible on routine disks. The patient is given clindamycin and gets worse. A question: did the lab report lie, or was something missing?

cues.text: A Staphylococcus aureus abscess isolate tests erythromycin-resistant and clindamycin-susceptible.
The patient is treated with clindamycin — and gets worse.
Was the report wrong? To see why, start with what “susceptible” really means.

scenes.title: Normal: MIC and MBC
scenes.altText: A row of tubes with doubling antibiotic concentrations (0.25–32 µg/mL), each inoculated with the same number of bacteria. After incubation, tubes with too little drug are turbid; the first clear tube is the MIC — the lowest concentration that inhibits visible growth (here 4 µg/mL). Subculturing clear tubes shows which concentration kills: the MBC is the lowest concentration that kills 99.9% of the inoculum (CLSI definition).

cues.text: Line up tubes with doubling amounts of antibiotic, and add the same number of bacteria to each.
After incubation, low-dose tubes are cloudy with growth. The first clear tube marks the minimum inhibitory concentration — the MIC. Here, 4.
Clear doesn’t mean dead. Subculture the clear tubes onto agar: the lowest concentration that kills 99.9 percent of the starting bacteria is the minimum bactericidal concentration — the MBC.
The MIC tells you what stops growth in the tube. It doesn’t yet tell you whether that drug will work in the patient.

props.label: In the tube ≠ in the patient

scenes.title: What changes: zones, breakpoints and S/I/R
scenes.altText: Disk diffusion plate: antibiotic diffuses out of each paper disk, making a gradient; bacteria grow only where the drug is too weak, leaving a clear zone. A large zone corresponds to a low MIC (inverse relationship). Breakpoint card: MIC or zone values are translated into susceptible / intermediate / resistant using breakpoints specific to the organism and drug; “S” means the MIC is at or below the breakpoint in vitro. Breakpoints are revised (CLSI M100 is updated yearly; e.g. minocycline breakpoints for Acinetobacter changed in the 2025 edition).

cues.text: In disk diffusion, paper disks soaked in antibiotic sit on a lawn of bacteria. The drug spreads outward, getting weaker with distance.
Bacteria grow only where the drug is too weak, so a clear zone forms. A bigger zone means a lower MIC — the two move in opposite directions.
To turn a zone or an MIC into a report, the lab uses breakpoints specific to that organism and that drug. Susceptible means the MIC is at or below the breakpoint — under test conditions.
Breakpoints change. CLSI publishes updated tables every year, so labs must use the current edition, not memorised numbers.

scenes.title: In the lab: the D-test
scenes.altText: D-test plate: an erythromycin disk (15 µg) and a clindamycin disk (2 µg) placed 15–20 mm apart on a S. aureus lawn. Erythromycin diffusing toward the clindamycin disk induces an erm methylase, so the bacteria near the erythromycin side become clindamycin-resistant and grow closer to the disk: the clindamycin zone flattens on that side into a “D”. A positive D-test means inducible MLSB resistance; clindamycin can fail during therapy. It is done on S. aureus isolates that are erythromycin-resistant and clindamycin-susceptible. A round zone (D-test negative) fits the efflux (MS) phenotype.

cues.text: The D-test is for staph that look erythromycin-resistant but clindamycin-susceptible. Place an erythromycin disk and a clindamycin disk 15 to 20 millimetres apart.
Erythromycin spreads toward the clindamycin disk and switches on an erm methylase gene in the bacteria nearby. Those bacteria now resist clindamycin too.
So the clindamycin zone gets flattened on the side facing erythromycin — it looks like the letter D. That’s inducible resistance: clindamycin may fail once treatment starts.
If the clindamycin zone stays round, the D-test is negative — erythromycin resistance is from an efflux pump that doesn’t affect clindamycin.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Trap card: “Clindamycin zone looks susceptible, so report S” is crossed out → “Check the shape: a D means inducible resistance.” Trap card: “A bigger zone means a higher MIC” is crossed out → “Inverse: bigger zone, lower MIC.” Trap card: “Use the same zone cut-off for every organism” is crossed out → “Breakpoints are organism- and drug-specific and revised yearly.”

cues.text: Trap one: a clindamycin zone of susceptible size isn’t the whole story. If it’s flattened into a D next to erythromycin, resistance is inducible.
Trap two: zone size and MIC run opposite ways. Bigger zone, lower MIC.
Trap three: there’s no universal cut-off. Breakpoints depend on the organism and the drug, and they’re revised every year.

props.title: ✗ “Clindamycin zone size is susceptible, so it’s fine.”
✗ “A bigger zone means a higher MIC.”
✗ “One zone cut-off fits every organism.”
lines: ✓ Organism- and drug-specific breakpoints, revised yearly

scenes.title: Big zone, small MIC — and mind the D
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Big zone, small MIC.” And “D is for Don’t trust clindamycin.” A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: big zone, small MIC. And D is for don’t trust clindamycin.

Where it breaks: zone size can’t be compared across different drugs or organisms; “susceptible” is an in-vitro category, and site, dose and biofilm still matter; and the exact reporting rules come from the current CLSI or EUCAST documents.

lines: Zones can’t be compared across drugs/organisms
“S” is in vitro — site, dose, biofilm matter · follow current CLSI/EUCAST

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “MIC = lowest concentration inhibiting visible growth; MBC = 99.9% kill; zone size is inverse to MIC”, “Use current organism-specific breakpoints; a D-shaped clindamycin zone = inducible resistance”.

cues.text: The MIC is the lowest concentration that stops visible growth and zone size runs opposite to it; interpret with current organism-specific breakpoints, and treat a D-shaped clindamycin zone as inducible resistance.

props.label: MIC: first clear tube · MBC: 99.9% kill · zone inverse to MIC
Current organism-specific breakpoints · D-zone = inducible resistance

explanation.what: Plain language: susceptibility tests find how much antibiotic it takes to stop a germ growing and whether that amount is achievable; the D-test reveals hidden clindamycin resistance. Scientific terms: MIC is the lowest concentration inhibiting visible growth; MBC the lowest killing 99.9% of the inoculum (CLSI); disk-diffusion zone diameters correlate inversely with MIC; breakpoints convert MICs/zones to S/I/R; erm-mediated inducible MLSB resistance flattens the clindamycin zone next to erythromycin.
explanation.why: Drug diffusing from a disk forms a concentration gradient; organisms with low MICs are inhibited farther from the disk. Erythromycin induces erm methylase, which modifies the ribosomal target shared by macrolides, lincosamides and streptogramin B.
explanation.measure: Dilution series: first clear well/tube = MIC; subculture for MBC. Interpret with current organism/drug-specific breakpoints (CLSI M100 is revised yearly; e.g. minocycline/Acinetobacter changes in 2025). D-test: erythromycin 15 µg and clindamycin 2 µg disks 15–20 mm apart on S. aureus that is erythromycin-R/clindamycin-S; flattened D = inducible MLSB (clindamycin may fail); round zone = MS (efflux) phenotype.
explanation.differs: MIC (inhibition) vs MBC (killing); zone diameter vs MIC (inverse); inducible MLSB (D+) vs constitutive MLSB (both resistant) vs MS phenotype (D−).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: MIC/MBC definitions, “bigger zone, lower MIC”, species-specific breakpoints, and D-test interpretation.

comparisons.title: D-test results
comparisons.distinguisher: Shape of the clindamycin zone next to erythromycin.

mnemonic.text: Big zone, small MIC — and D is for “don’t trust clindamycin”.
mnemonic.explanation: Zone diameter and MIC are inversely related; a D-shaped zone signals inducible clindamycin resistance.
mnemonic.limitation: Zones cannot be compared across drugs or organisms; “S” is an in-vitro category; reporting follows current CLSI/EUCAST rules.

β-lactamase, ESBL and carbapenemase testing are not covered here.

questions.stem: In a broth dilution series (0.25–32 µg/mL), tubes up to 2 µg/mL are turbid and tubes from 4 µg/mL upward are clear. What is the MIC?

options.rationale: Correct. The MIC is the lowest concentration with no visible growth.
Incorrect. That tube still shows growth.
Incorrect. That is the highest concentration, not the lowest inhibitory one.

options.text: It cannot be read without subculture
options.rationale: Incorrect. Subculture is needed for the MBC, not the MIC.

questions.stem: An erythromycin-resistant, clindamycin-susceptible S. aureus shows a clindamycin zone flattened on the side facing the erythromycin disk. What does this indicate?

options.text: Inducible clindamycin (MLSB) resistance — clindamycin may fail
options.rationale: Correct. Erythromycin induces erm methylase, producing the D-shaped zone.
Incorrect. The MS phenotype gives a round clindamycin zone.

options.text: Disks placed too close; repeat without interpretation
options.rationale: Incorrect. Proximity (15–20 mm) is intended to reveal induction.
Incorrect. Flattening indicates antagonism/induction, not synergy.

questions.stem: A 13-mm zone is measured around a cefepime disk for Pseudomonas aeruginosa. How should it be interpreted?

options.text: Using the current organism- and drug-specific breakpoint for P. aeruginosa and cefepime
options.rationale: Correct. Breakpoints are specific to each organism–drug pair and are revised.

options.text: As susceptible, because any zone above 10 mm is susceptible
options.rationale: Incorrect. There is no universal zone cut-off.

options.text: By comparing it with the zone for a different antibiotic on the same plate
options.rationale: Incorrect. Zones of different drugs are not comparable.

options.text: As resistant, because smaller zones always mean resistance
options.rationale: Incorrect. Whether 13 mm is small depends on the breakpoint.

claims.text: MIC = lowest concentration inhibiting visible growth; MBC = 99.9% kill (CLSI).
Zone diameter inversely related to MIC.
Organism/drug-specific breakpoints convert to S/I/R; S = MIC ≤ breakpoint in vitro; CLSI M100 revised yearly.
D-test: E 15 µg + CC 2 µg, 15–20 mm apart; D shape = inducible erm MLSB, clindamycin may fail; round = MS.
CLSI: report clindamycin as resistant when the D-test is positive; BMD at 35 °C, 16–20 h is the reference method.
